content: Tansy, scientifically known as Tanacetum vulgare, is a perennial herbaceous plant belonging to the aster family. It is native to temperate regions of Europe and Asia but has been introduced to other parts of the world, where it has sometimes become invasive. The plant is also referred to by various names, including Common Tansy, Bitter Buttons, Cow Bitter, Mugwort, and Golden Buttons. The plant is characterized by its finely divided, compound leaves and yellow, button-like flowers. It has a sturdy, erect stem that is somewhat reddish in color, smooth in texture, and grows to a height of 50 to 150 cm, branching near the top. The leaves are alternately arranged, measuring 10 to 15 cm in length, and are pinnately lobed. Each leaf is divided into approximately seven pairs of segments or lobes, which are further subdivided into smaller lobes with serrated edges, giving the foliage a fern-like appearance. The flowers are round, flat-topped, and yellow, forming terminal clusters that bloom from mid to late summer. The plant emits a scent reminiscent of camphor, with subtle notes of rosemary. Both the leaves and flowers are considered toxic if ingested in large quantities due to the presence of thujone, a volatile compound also found in absinthe, which can induce convulsions. Interestingly, certain insects, such as the tansy beetle, have developed resistance to the plant's toxicity and rely on it as their primary food source. Tansy is native to Eurasia and is widespread across mainland Europe, though it is absent from Siberia and some Mediterranean islands. Historical records suggest that the ancient Greeks were among the first to cultivate tansy for medicinal purposes. By 1525, it was recognized in Britain as an essential garden herb, referred to as Tansey. Historically, tansy was used as a culinary ingredient, particularly as a flavoring agent in puddings and omelets, though its use in modern cuisine is rare. In the past, it was highly regarded for its taste, with herbalist John Gerarde describing it as pleasant in taste and recommending tansy sweetmeats as a remedy for gout when consumed daily on an empty stomach. In Yorkshire, tansy was traditionally combined with caraway seeds to make biscuits served at funerals. Additionally, Jack Daniel, the founder of the Tennessee whiskey brand, reportedly enjoyed drinking his whiskey with sugar and crushed tansy leaves. Tansy has a long history of use in traditional medicine. Irish folklore from the mid-19th century mentions bathing in a solution of tansy and salt as a remedy for joint pain. Bitter tea made from the blossoms of T. vulgare has been used for centuries as an anthelmintic (a treatment for intestinal worms). During Lent, tansy cakes were traditionally consumed due to the belief that eating fish during this period caused intestinal worms. It is important to note that only T. vulgare is used in medicinal preparations, as all tansy species are toxic, and overdoses can be fatal. The dried flowering herb of Tanacetum has been used ethnomedically to treat migraines, neuralgia, and rheumatism, as well as for its anthelmintic properties, though its use should be supervised by a qualified herbalist to avoid toxicity. Historically, tansy was also employed for its emmenagogue effects (stimulating menstruation), but it has been associated with cases of miscarriage, making it unsafe for use during pregnancy. Beyond its medicinal and culinary applications, tansy has been used for various practical purposes. In England, it was traditionally placed in windows to repel flies, and sprigs were added to bedding and linens to deter pests. The plant has also been used by traditional dyers to produce a golden-yellow pigment. Its dried flowers are often used in floral arrangements. As a companion plant, tansy is thought to repel a variety of pests, including ants, cucumber beetles, Japanese beetles, squash bugs, and certain flying insects. It is commonly planted alongside cucurbits (such as cucumbers and squash), roses, or berries for this purpose. Tansy has also been referenced in art and literature. A 19th-century poem by John Clare, titled The Cross Roads; or, The Haymaker's Story, describes the beauty of tansy and other herbs in a nostalgic depiction of a garden. The poem highlights the plant's prominence in the natural and cultural landscape of the time.
